name: North Korea

findings.controller: Huawei (equipment supplied via Panda International Information Technology)
findings.local_actor: Koryolink (CHEO Technology: Orascom and Korea Post and Telecommunications Corp.)
findings.summary: Leaked internal documents reported by the Washington Post indicate Huawei, working through state-owned Panda International, supplied base stations and handled integration, software, managed services and encryption work for Koryolink over at least eight years.
findings.analyst_inference: Both opened sources relay the same Washington Post leak (the Post itself was not opened); corroborated on the mechanical rule only, reviewer may disagree. Huawei denied any business presence. Tier 5 because Koryolink operated nationally (~3m subscribers per 2015 reporting). TechRadar says Huawei no longer maintains Koryolink; still_current not confirmed, so the map halves this pre-2020 finding. Date 2008 is the JV launch; work reportedly ran from about 2006-08 for 8+ years.

findings.local_actor: Koryolink and Kang Song NET (Ministry of Information Industry)
findings.summary: Reports from late 2023 say North Korea began importing used Huawei equipment through China to upgrade 3G base stations in Pyongyang and other cities; Kangsong's 4G service, launched in Pyongyang in September 2023, is reportedly built on it.
findings.analyst_inference: Mechanically corroborated, but every opened source traces the Huawei claim to one anonymous Daily NK source; the Daily NK 4G launch article opened does not name a vendor. Confidence held low for that reason. Tier 4 for equipment being installed; tier 5 not claimed because the 4G-vendor link is unconfirmed. Grey-market gear likely gets no vendor updates, so prc control is weaker than the vendor rule implies; a reviewer may prefer pole null. Implies sanctions-evading import; coded as deployment, not enforcement.

findings.summary: A China Unicom connection has carried North Korea's international internet traffic, via the ISP Star JV, since 2010; apart from a short Intelsat satellite route from 2012, it was the only link until October 2017.
findings.analyst_inference: Layer networks (international transit). Pole prc because China Unicom, a PRC state operator, can switch the uplink off. Only confirmed to 2017; still_current not checked this run, so the map halves it.

findings.summary: Russian carrier TransTeleCom began providing North Korea a second internet connection in October 2017, presumably over fibre along the railway crossing the Friendship Bridge between Khasan and Tumangang, ending China Unicom's monopoly on the uplink.
findings.analyst_inference: Russia is coded third (neither US nor PRC). Tier 5 because routes were live in routing tables. Date taken from 38 North's URL date and its note of a Sunday appearance; the Telecoms.com piece is dated 2 October. Telecoms.com relies on 38 North, so independence is partial. still_current not checked this run.

findings.controller: Orascom Telecom Media and Technology (Egypt), 75% owner-operator of Koryolink
findings.local_actor: Koryolink (CHEO Technology); Korea Post and Telecommunications Corp.
findings.reversal_of: Orascom's 75% control of the Koryolink 3G joint venture
findings.summary: Orascom reported losing control of its 75%-owned Koryolink venture and wrote it off after failing to repatriate profits; the state had launched a rival carrier and sought majority control of any merger.
findings.analyst_inference: Reversal of a foreign (Egyptian, third) operator's control, not of the equipment vendor; pole third on the operator-as-controller reading, reviewer may prefer pole null for networks. Reason coded commercial: sources cite blocked repatriation and currency rules, with sanctions only a partial factor, and the state's rival carrier, so it does not meet the brief's bar for sanctions. A reviewer may judge sanctions or geopolitical. Pre-2020; current status of Orascom's claim not checked.

facilities.null_reason: no dedicated search; no data-centre or AI-campus project surfaced in network or AI-research searches

silicon.null_reason: 38 North (opened) identifies no North Korean accelerator hardware and notes sanctions limit procurement; US embargo already covered by global layer

models.null_reason: no named North Korean LLM or adoption of a foreign frontier model found in 2 searches; NK Pro (July 2025) argues Pyongyang will struggle to build LLMs

applications.null_reason: 38 North reports only domestic claims of neural-network features in Azalea phones and Yalu River surveillance cameras, with no foreign stack or scale stated

research_gaps: TechRadar (relaying the Washington Post) says Kang Song launched in 2013 with ZTE support; not confirmed by any opened source. Who supplied Kangsong's original 3G network?
Is the China Unicom uplink still active, and is the TransTeleCom link still in use after 2017? Any newer satellite or Russian routes since 2023-24?
Can a second source independent of Daily NK confirm the 2023 used-Huawei upgrade and tie it to the 4G rollout?
Did Orascom ever regain control or sell its Koryolink stake, and did the Koryolink/Kangsong merger happen?
38 North (Aug 2024) on North Korea's international AI-research network, including Chinese co-authors, was seen in search only; does it show any foreign model or compute access?
Any domestic data centre for the Kwangmyong intranet, and its hardware origin?
